evidence: A silhouette suppresses color and texture while retaining projected body contour. Its compactness supports effective sequence processing in GaitSet, GaitPart, and GaitGL. Clothing and carried objects nevertheless change the contour itself, and coherent segmentation errors may persist across frames. GaitEdge connects segmentation and alignment to recognition; analysis of cropping further shows how normalization affects the resulting evidence.

Skeletons retain articulation with little texture or contour information. GPGait combines body-coordinate processing with graph learning; SkeletonGait renders joints as maps and uses convolutions. These routes separate the choice of skeletal evidence from graph topology. OpenGait's reduced-channel SkeletonGait remains competitive at a parameter count close to GPGait, although pose sources and encoding choices also differ. Shared pose-processing baselines help localize these effects. Both routes remain exposed to occlusion and upstream estimation error.

method: Gaitset: Regarding gait as a set for cross-view gait recognition
evidence: Set pooling offers variable-length aggregation without requiring temporal alignment. In an idealized frame-wise encoder followed by symmetric pooling, z=\!(Pool_t=1^T(x_t)), the representation is invariant to frame permutations. This simplifies aggregation when ordering or phase alignment is unreliable, while discarding the order of otherwise identical frames. Local temporal operations before pooling can retain ordering information within their receptive fields.

A published GaitMax ablation illustrates why the temporal question benefits from condition-specific analysis. Its kinematic branch exceeds the order-invariant semantic branch by 6.7 points on CCPG clothing change, while the semantic branch leads by 2.7 points on bag carrying. Fusion improves mean rank-1 to 89.8%, but its clothing score of 85.4% remains below the kinematic branch's 87.6%. These ablation settings differ from the final comparison in Table III. The ablation reveals condition-dependent complementarity between semantic and kinematic cues. Fusion should therefore be assessed against the strongest individual branch for each condition as well as by its aggregate score. A repeated-frame control would test whether a single frame supports the gain; frame shuffling would probe order dependence, and matched-duration sampling would probe temporal coverage. Applying these controls within each covariate condition would help distinguish useful temporal evidence from architectural sensitivity to sequence order.

A common recipe combines identity classification with metric learning. For an anchor z_a, positive z_p, and negative z_n, a representative triplet objective is L_ tri=[d(z_a,z_p)-d(z_a,z_n)+m]_+, where m is a margin. Classification separates training identities; metric learning shapes relations used to match unseen people. Part-wise heads, normalization, and batch construction determine how these objectives act on gait sequences.

Persistent occlusion instead forces reliance on remaining evidence or inferred structure, whose confidence should reflect that it was not directly observed.

Local motion models such as GaitPart and DyGait can reduce reliance on affected regions, while semantic and structural inputs support body–object separation. These are partial remedies: excluding the object's pixels does not undo the resulting change in walking dynamics. CCGR's combined conditions provide a broader test than bag presence alone.

method: Open-set biometrics: Beyond good closed-set models
evidence: Rank-1 measures the first match; mAP summarizes retrieval across relevant gallery items; mINP emphasizes the last relevant item's rank. Verification and open-set identification additionally require a rejection operating point. Verification can report true-accept rate (TAR) at fixed false-accept rates (FAR), while open-set identification can report false-negative identification rate (FNIR) at fixed false-positive identification rates (FPIR), with gallery size and mated/non-mated probe composition specified. Holding a validation threshold fixed while varying gallery size or acquisition tests a different capability from recomputing the best threshold for each test set. Subject-level uncertainty and the fraction of retained probes show how calibration and abstention affect reliability and coverage.

Across these dimensions, a practical comparison includes observation duration, upstream extraction, embedding computation, and gallery search. GaitMax, for example, separates backbone and head costs and specifies frame count and resolution. Per-frame computation differs from sequence latency, which also includes waiting for useful observations; deployment cost includes both upstream feature extraction and the recognition head. These constraints connect the methodological choices to the uses considered next.

method: FineRehab: A Multi-modality and Multi-task Dataset for Rehabilitation Analysis
evidence: Action-based rehabilitation analysis evaluates prescribed movements with known intent and expert quality labels. FineRehab, for example, combines visual and inertial observations for exercise recognition and multidimensional quality assessment. Walking offers a complementary opportunity: it is frequent in daily life and can support repeated observation with less task-specific instruction. Video-based scoliosis studies, ScoliGaitX, and recent skeletal-health modeling demonstrate interest in this direction. Together, these studies motivate task-specific models for repeated assessment of everyday walking.

Identity-pretrained features can encode a personal baseline, but matching invariance may suppress asymmetry or temporal change needed for assessment. A key comparison is whether identity pretraining improves longitudinal change detection over action- or pose-pretrained features under matched labels and capacity. Task-specific readouts could preserve this distinction. Comparing a patient's change with their own baseline, alongside population-level assessment, would help test whether the representation separates stable personal style from clinically relevant variation. Generative approaches such as GAITGen likewise need condition-relevant biomechanics, beyond visually plausible walking.

method: FollowMe: A Robust Person Following Framework Based on Visual Re-Identification and Gestures
evidence: Human detection, pose, gestures, tracking, and appearance ReID already support robot interaction. FollowMe integrates ReID and gesture recognition with navigation; online continual ReID adapts person-following features to changing viewpoints and appearance. Gait could complement these systems when a person faces away or facial detail is unavailable, particularly during reacquisition after occlusion. Existing components establish a feasible integration context, while gait's incremental value still needs robot-based evaluation.

Protection can act on videos, derived representations, templates, or access to outputs. Each protection claim should specify the released object, the adversary's access, and the downstream utility to be retained. Adversarial gait methods manipulate temporal or contour information, while GaitProtector uses diffusion-latent optimization for gait de-identification. GaitEditor explores a complementary route through semantic attribute editing in a GAN latent space, using stronger and repeated edits to reduce identity recognizability while retaining visually plausible walking sequences. Their protection depends on attacker access, transfer to unseen recognizers, and survival through compression and re-extraction. Evaluation can examine transfer to independent recognizers, adaptation to protected data, and linkage across repeated releases. For example, testing a new recognizer trained on protected outputs would ask whether identity information remains learnable, beyond whether protection transfers to an already trained model. Repeated-release tests should also examine whether observations that are individually difficult to identify become linkable when combined.
